fatal_errors: The proposed intervention modifies TiVNbTa, whereas the target intervention compares equiatomic CrFeTaVW with CrFeTiVW by replacing Ta with Ti.
The predicted benefit—30–50% higher yield strength at 1273 K—is not supported by the target study, which did not report high-temperature mechanical testing or strength improvement.

The claimed solid-solution-strengthening mechanism conflicts with the target finding that Ta and Ti have similar atomic radii and that Ti substitution primarily changes phase constitution and segregation behavior.
The response omits the central comparison between conventional MD and hybrid MD/Monte Carlo atom-swap simulations, as well as the associated lower-energy configurations and W-related segregation.
It does not address the target thermal-transport result: Ta-to-Ti substitution leaves thermal diffusivity nearly unchanged, with both alloys substantially less diffusive than W and CuCrZr.
No prior HEA evidence is actually cited or connected causally to the proposed intervention.
explanation: The response recognizes the broad divertor-interlayer problem and proposes a compositionally controlled experiment, but it does not reconstruct the studied material system, computational intervention, processing route, mechanism, or measured outcomes. Its Ta-to-Ti idea only superficially resembles the target substitution because it is applied within TiVNbTa rather than CrFeTaVW. The asserted strengthening, increased lattice strain, suppression of phase transformations, and 30–50% strength gain are speculative and unsupported. Although the alloy series and mechanical tests could falsify the performance claim, the experiment does not directly test the proposed short-range-order or dislocation-mobility mechanism and omits thermal diffusivity, segregation metrics, and MD-versus-hybrid-MC controls.
